extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of classical Euclidean geometry (students, teachers, mathematicians)
extracted.subtask_description: Instructions, constructions, and foundational definitions from Euclid (Elements, Book IV–start of Book V) for inscribing/circumscribing regular polygons, inscribing/circumscribing circles, and the definitions/axioms/propositions about ratios and magnitudes. Useful for performing or verifying classical geometric constructions and reasoning about proportions.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XI — To inscribe an equilateral and equiangular pentagon in a given circle
rubrics_metrics.description: Let ABCDE be the given circle; it is required to inscribe an equilateral and equiangular pentagon in the circle. Describe an isosceles triangle FGH having each of the angles at G, H double of the angle at F; in the circle ABCDE inscribe the triangle ACD equiangular to FGH so that angle CAD equals angle at F, and each of ACD, CDA equal to angle at G or H; bisect ACD and CDA by CE, DB; join AB, BC, DE, EA. ABCDE is the pentagon required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because each of ACD, CDA is double of CAD and are bisected by CE, DB, the five angles DAC, ACE, ECD, CDB, BDA are equal; equal angles stand upon equal circumferences so the five circumferences AB, BC, CD, DE, EA are equal and hence the five straight lines AB, BC, CD, DE, EA are equal — the pentagon is equilateral. Equiangularity established by comparing circumferences and angles (BAE = AED, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XII — To describe an equilateral and equiangular pentagon about a given circle
rubrics_metrics.description: Let ABCDE be the given circle; required to describe an equilateral and equiangular pentagon about it. Take points A,B,C,D,E on circle as in last proposition so the circumferences AB, BC, CD, DE, EA are equal; through A,B,C,D,E draw GH, HK, KL, LM, MG touching the circle; take centre F and join FB, FK, FC, FL, FD. Show corresponding right angles and congruent triangles to deduce equal straight lines (GH,HK,... etc.) and equal angles, hence GHKLM is equilateral and equiangular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use properties of tangents (radius perpendicular to tangent at point of contact), right triangles, and equality of circumferences to deduce equal segments and angles; then conclude the pentagon formed by the tangents is equilateral and equiangular and circumscribes the circle.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XIII — To inscribe a circle in a given equilateral and equiangular pentagon
rubrics_metrics.description: Let ABCDE be the given equilateral and equiangular pentagon; required to inscribe a circle in it. Bisect angles BCD, CDE by CF, DF; from intersection F draw FB, FA, FE. Bisect other angles similarly and draw perpendiculars from F to the sides AB, BC, CD, DE, EA. These perpendiculars (FG, FH, FK, FL, FM) are equal; the circle described with centre F and radius one of these perpendiculars touches all five sides and is inscribed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use congruence of triangles formed by equal sides and bisected angles to show perpendiculars from F to each side are equal; a circle with that radius centred at F will touch each side since the foot is at right angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XIV — To describe a circle about a given equilateral and equiangular pentagon
rubrics_metrics.description: Let ABCDE be the given equilateral and equiangular pentagon; required to describe a circle about it. Bisect angles BCD and CDE by CF and DF meet at F; draw FB, FA, FE. Show CF = FD and similarly FB = FA = FE = FC = FD; the circle with centre F and radius one of these passes through all five vertices and is described about the pentagon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use equality of angles and bisectors to deduce equality of distances from the common intersection point to the vertices, then draw circle with that radius to circumscribe the pentagon.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XV — To inscribe an equilateral and equiangular hexagon in a given circle
rubrics_metrics.description: Let ABCDEF be the given circle; required to inscribe an equilateral and equiangular hexagon. Find centre G and draw diameter AGD; from D as centre, with distance DC describe circle EGCH, join EG, CG and extend to B,F, then join polygon sides AB, BC, CD, DE, EF, FA. Show triangles like EGD equilateral and that the six central angles are equal, hence the six circumferences and straight lines AB..FA are equal — hexagon is equilateral and equiangular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use center properties and equal radii to form equilateral triangles and deduce that each central angle is 1/6 of full circle; equal circumferences imply equal chord lengths and hence equal sides of hexagon. Corollary: side of hexagon equals the semi-diameter (radius).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary (to Prop. XV) — Side of inscribed regular hexagon equals semicircle radius
rubrics_metrics.description: From Prop. XV: the side of the hexagon is equal to the straight line from the centre, that is, to the semi-diameter of the circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate consequence of the construction and equality of triangles used in Prop. XV.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XVI — To inscribe an equilateral and equiangular quindecagon in a given circle
rubrics_metrics.description: Let ABCD be given circle; let AC be side of equilateral triangle inscribed (third part of circumference) and AB side of equilateral and equiangular pentagon (fifth part). Then circumferences split into fifteenths: ABC contains five fifteenths and AB contains three; BC their difference contains two; bisect BC at E so BE and EC are each fifteenth of whole circumference; placing such equal straight lines around circle produces an equilateral and equiangular quindecagon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine constructions of triangle and pentagon to partition the circle into 15 equal arcs by differences and bisection; then place equal chords around the circle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition I (Book V) — Part and greater magnitude (measure definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A less magnitude is said to be a part of a greater magnitude, when the less measures the greater, that is, when the less is contained a certain number of times exactly in the greater.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives the notion of 'part' by exact integer measure; foundational for ratios and multiples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition II (Book V) — Multiple
rubrics_metrics.description: A greater magnitude is said to be a multiple of a less, when the greater is measured by the less, that is, when the greater contains the less a certain number of times exactly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Companion to Definition I; used to relate magnitudes via integer multiples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition III (Book V) — Ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: Ratio is a mutual relation of two magnitudes of the same kind to one another, in respect of quantity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduces ratio concept as relation between same-kind magnitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition IV (Book V) — When magnitudes have a ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: Magnitudes are said to have a ratio to one another, when the less can be multiplied so as to exceed the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion ensuring comparability (Archimedean property) needed for ratio theory in Book V.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition V (Book V) — Equality of ratios via equimultiples
rubrics_metrics.description: The first of four magnitudes is said to have the same ratio to the second which the third has to the fourth, when any equimultiples whatsoever of the first and third being taken, and any equimultiples whatsoever of the second and fourth; if the multiple of the first be less than that of the second, the multiple of the third is also less than that of the fourth; or equal to equal; or greater to greater.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Euclid's definition of proportionality using the method of equimultiples (Eudoxusian approach), foundational for rigorous handling of incommensurable magnitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition VI (Book V) — Proportionals
rubrics_metrics.description: Magnitudes which have the same ratio are called proportionals. Note: when four magnitudes are proportionals, it is usually expressed by saying 'the first is to the second, as the third to the fourth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminology for working with ratios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition VII (Book V) — Greater/less ratio comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: When of the equimultiples of four magnitudes (taken as in Def. V) the multiple of the first is greater than that of the second, but the multiple of the third is not greater than the multiple of the fourth; then the first is said to have to the second a greater ratio than the third has to the fourth; conversely the third has to the fourth a less ratio than the first to the second.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition permits ordering of ratios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition VIII (Book V) — Analogy / proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogy, or proportion, is the similitude of ratios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminology linking proportionality with analogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition IX (Book V) — Minimum terms in proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportion consists in three terms at least.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that proportion involves at least three magnitudes in Euclid's exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition X (Book V) — Duplicate ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: When three magnitudes are proportionals, the first is said to have to the third the duplicate ratio of that which it has to the second.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduces compounded (squared) ratios notion by term count.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition XI (Book V) — Triplicate and higher ratios (continual proportionals)
rubrics_metrics.description: When four magnitudes are continual proportionals, the first is said to have to the fourth the triplicate ratio of that which it has to the second, and so on (quadruplicate etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extends the duplicative concept to more terms; note about increasing denomination by unity for any number of proportionals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition A — Compound ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: When there are any number of magnitudes of the same kind, the first is said to have to the last of them the ratio compounded of the ratio which the first has to the second, and of the ratio which the second has to the third, ... and so on to the last magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives formal meaning of product (composition) of successive ratios; illustrated with magnitudes A,B,C,D and equivalence to other ratio chains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition XII (Book V) — Homologous antecedents/consequents and technical words
rubrics_metrics.description: In proportionals, the antecedent terms are called homologous to one another, as also the consequents to one another. Geometers use technical words to signify ways of changing order/magnitude of proportionals while preserving proportionality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets up vocabulary for permutations and transformations of proportional statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition XIII (Book V) — Permutando / alternando
rubrics_metrics.description: Permutando, or alternando: when there are four proportionals, it is inferred that the first has the same ratio to the third which the second has to the fourth; i.e., the first is to the third as the second to the fourth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Names one allowed transformation of proportional relations (see Prop. 16 of Book V).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition XIV (Book V) — Invertendo
rubrics_metrics.description: Invertendo, by inversion: when there are four proportionals, it is inferred that the second is to the first as the fourth to the third.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Another transformation useful in proportion manipulations (see Prop. B, Book V).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition XV (Book V) — Componendo
rubrics_metrics.description: Componendo, by composition: when there are four proportionals, it is inferred that the first together with the second is to the second, as the third together with the fourth is to the fourth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operation adding antecedent and consequent pairs; referenced to Prop. 18 of Book V.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition XVI (Book V) — Dividendo
rubrics_metrics.description: Dividendo, by division: when there are four proportionals, it is inferred that the excess of the first above the second is to the second as the excess of the third above the fourth is to the fourth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operation forming difference ratios; referenced to Prop. 17 of Book V.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition XVII (Book V) — Convertendo
rubrics_metrics.description: Convertendo, by conversion: when there are four proportionals, it is inferred that the first is to its excess above the second as the third to its excess above the fourth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Another proportional transformation (see Prop. 5^ book 5 [?]; Euclid references).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition XVIII (Book V) — Ex sequali (from equality of distance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ex sequali (sc. distantia), or ex aequo: when there is any number of magnitudes more than two, and as many others, so that they are proportionals when taken two and two of each rank, it is inferred that the first is to the last of the first rank as the first is to the last of the others. Two kinds arise from differing order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions for comparing ordered sequences of proportionals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition XIX (Book V) — Ex aquali (from equality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ex aquali, from equality: used when the first magnitude is to the second of the first rank as the first is to the second of the other rank; and so on — called ordinate proportion. Demonstrated in Prop. 22 of Book V.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminology for certain proportional correspondences and theorems that follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition XX (Book V) — Ex aequali in perturbate (in disorderly proportion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ex aequali, in proportione perturbata, seu inordinata; from equality in perturbate or disorderly proportion: used when correspondences of ranks are cross-ordered (first to second of first rank as last-but-one to last of second rank, etc.). Demonstrated in Prop. 23 of Book V.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminology for cross-order proportional inferences used later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom I (Book V) — Equimultiples of equal magnitudes are equal
rubrics_metrics.description: Equimultiples of the same, or of equal magnitudes, are equal to one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foundational axiom (used e.g., in Archimedean style arguments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom II (Book V) — Equality by equimultiples
rubrics_metrics.description: Those magnitudes of which the same, or equal magnitudes, are equimultiples, are equal to one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Companion axiom about equality via equimultiples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom III (Book V) — Multiple ordering
rubrics_metrics.description: A multiple of a greater magnitude is greater than the same multiple of a less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to compare magnitudes via equal multipliers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom IV (Book V) — Multiple comparison implies base comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: That magnitude of which a multiple is greater than the same multiple of another, is greater than that other magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning principle to deduce ordering of magnitudes from ordering of multiples.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. I (Book V) — Equimultiples preserve multiple relations across groups
rubrics_metrics.description: If any number of magnitudes be equimultiples of as many, each of each; whatsoever multiple any one of them is of its part, the same multiple shall all the first magnitudes be of all the other. (Formal statement and proof using partition into parts equal to parts of the compared group.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows that equality of 'how many of' relations is preserved when aggregating multiple magnitudes and their corresponding parts; fundamental lemma in Euclid's equimultiple approach to ratios.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. II (Book V) — Sum of multiples preserves multiplicity relation
rubrics_metrics.description: If the first magnitude be the same multiple of the second that the third is of the fourth, and the fifth the same multiple of the second that the sixth is of the fourth; then the first together with the fifth shall be the same multiple of the second that the third together with the sixth is of the fourth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to combine multiplicative relations across sums (corollary extends to any number of parts).

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. III (Book V) — Equimultiples of proportionals are proportionals
rubrics_metrics.description: If the first be the same multiple of the second which the third is of the fourth; and if of the first and third there be taken equimultiples, these shall be equimultiples, the one of the second, and the other of the fourth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows equimultiples of magnitudes with equal ratio yield corresponding equimultiples in the other magnitudes; technical lemma in proportional reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. IV (Book V) — Equimultiples maintain ratio across any equimultiples
rubrics_metrics.description: If the first of four magnitudes has the same ratio to the second which the third hath to the fourth, then any equimultiples whatever of the first and third shall have the same ratio to any equimultiples of the second and fourth, viz. the equimultiple of the first shall have the same ratio to that of the second which the equimultiple of the third has to that of the fourth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generalizes Def. V by allowing arbitrary equimultiples; proof uses taking further equimultiples and the ordering relations of greater/equal/less to conclude the ratio equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. V (Book V) — Remainder multiple relation preservation
rubrics_metrics.description: If one magnitude be the same multiple of another which a magnitude taken from the first is of a magnitude taken from the other; the remainder shall be the same multiple of the remainder that the whole is of the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relates multiplicative relations after subtraction; proven by constructing matching multiples and comparing remainders.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. VI (Book V) — Remainders from equimultiples are equal or multiples
rubrics_metrics.description: If two magnitudes be equimultiples of two others, and if equimultiples of these be taken from the first two, the remainders are either equal to these others, or equimultiples of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides case analysis showing remainders after removing equimultiples are themselves equal or multiples; used in later proportional arguments.
